ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure is a single-stage NPN transistor common-emitter amplifier circuit. The base is voltage-divider biased by two resistors, and the input signal is applied to the base through a coupling capacitor; the collector is connected to +12 V through a resistor, and the output is taken from the collector through a coupling capacitor; the emitter has an emitter resistor connected to ground, and the capacitor C_E is connected from the emitter node to ground, forming an AC bypass with the emitter resistor. Reasoning: In the original mid-frequency small-signal equivalent circuit, the coupling capacitors and bypass capacitor can approximately be regarded as AC short circuits, so C_E will AC-bypass the emitter resistor, making the emitter close to AC ground, and the magnitude of the common-emitter voltage gain is relatively large. If C_E is removed, the emitter resistor is no longer bypassed and will appear in the small-signal emitter loop, producing emitter negative feedback/emitter degeneration, which increases the equivalent emitter impedance. According to the common gain relationship, the gain magnitude is higher when bypassed, and when not bypassed the gain approximately contains the r_e + R_E term, so the voltage gain magnitude becomes smaller. Therefore, after removing C_E, the mid-frequency small-signal voltage gain decreases.

From the question, compare midband voltage gain before and after removing C_E. Replace the capacitors by AC shorts for the original midband circuit: C_E shorts the emitter resistor, so the emitter is nearly at AC ground and gain is high. Then remove C_E in the small-signal model: the emitter resistor is no longer bypassed and appears in series with the intrinsic emitter resistance, increasing the effective emitter impedance. Apply the standard gain formulas to conclude the magnitude of the AC small-signal midband voltage gain decreases.

method.method_draft: First describe the image and locate C_E as the emitter bypass capacitor. From the question, consider the effect of removing this capacitor. With C_E installed at midband, signal current can pass through the low reactance of C_E to ground, so the emitter node is nearly fixed for AC and little emitter-degeneration feedback occurs. When C_E is removed, the signal current must flow through the emitter resistor, causing an AC emitter voltage that moves with the base signal. This reduces the effective base-emitter signal and hence reduces collector-current variation and collector output swing. Therefore the amplifier's midband voltage gain decreases.
